blocks.text: Imaging methods that use ionising radiation rely on how radiation interacts with matter: as photons pass through tissue they may be absorbed or scattered, and the pattern of energy deposited and attenuated produces measurable signals at a detector. In nuclear medicine the radiation starts inside the patient, from an administered radiopharmaceutical, so the signal shows how the body is working (function) rather than only its shape (anatomy). In single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT), a gamma-emitting tracer is introduced into the body and a rotating gamma camera records many views, which are reconstructed into cross-sectional images of tracer distribution, giving 3D information about blood flow and organ function.

Positron emission tomography (PET) extends this idea using positron-emitting tracers (Fig 20.10 shows a PET scanner). A small amount of radioactive tracer is injected into a vein; the blood carries it, and it builds up more in very active tissues, such as many cancers and working parts of the brain and heart. As the unstable nuclei of the tracer decay they emit positrons. Each positron travels only a short distance before meeting an electron in nearby tissue; the two annihilate, and their mass is converted into two gamma-ray photons that move in opposite directions. A ring of detectors around the patient detects these photon pairs in coincidence (arriving at the same instant) and sends the signals to a computer, which locates each event and constructs an image showing where the tracer has collected (Fig 20.11). Brighter areas show higher tracer concentration and therefore higher tissue activity.

blocks.alt: Left: a positron emitter, an atom whose nucleus gives out a positron among orbiting electrons; the positron meets an electron and they annihilate, sending two gamma-rays in opposite directions. Centre: a PET scanner ring with the patient on its couch and gamma-rays from the patient to the ring. A curved arrow leads to a computer display on the right.
blocks.caption: Figure 20.11: Schematic diagram of PET-scanning (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 20.11).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 20.11 reads 'Nuctrus' and 'Y-RAYS' and puts the positron-electron annihilation label on the arrow to the computer. They are nucleus and gamma-rays, and the annihilation takes place inside the body, where it is labelled above.

So PET is a non-invasive technique that images metabolic and biochemical activity at the cellular and molecular level, making it very valuable for early cancer detection and staging, evaluating brain function and identifying heart abnormalities before clear anatomical changes appear.

Medical physics is also very important in the treatment and diagnosis of cancer, especially through radiotherapy, which uses high-energy radiation to kill tumour cells with minimal harm to healthy tissue. Radiation therapy has two main approaches: teletherapy, in which radiation is delivered from a machine outside the body, and brachytherapy, in which a radioactive source is placed inside or close to the tumour. Medical physicists are part of the oncology team: they specialise in equipment quality assurance, calculating treatment times, planning treatment and mapping the dose distribution in the cancerous region, working with radiation oncologists, dosimetrists and laboratory technicians to make every treatment safe and effective.
